prompt.context: Our client is a large industrial equipment company with four business units: airplane engines, industrial cranes, oil drilling equipment, and recreational aircraft. The recreational aircraft division makes small planes like Cessnas that people fly for fun. The division was doing well in the 1980s but started declining in the 1990s and was shut down in 2000. The people were moved to other divisions and the plant was closed. It is now 2009.
prompt.question:
Part I: What issues do you think are important to consider in assessing the key drivers, opportunities, and risks for this company?

Part II: The client is wondering whether they should get back into the recreational aircraft market or sell off the assets and get out for good. What should we consider, and what is your recommendation?

clarifying_info.q: How large is the US population?
What share of the population has a pilot's license?
clarifying_info.a: 1% of the population has a pilot's license.

clarifying_info.q: What fraction of pilots have high enough income to own a plane?
clarifying_info.a: 1/3 of pilots have high enough income to actually own a plane or part of a plane.

clarifying_info.q: How do high-income pilots typically acquire planes?
clarifying_info.a: 10% buy their own plane; the remaining 90% belong to flying clubs where they share ownership with other pilots. Assume 10 pilots per plane in clubs.

clarifying_info.q: How long is the useful life of a recreational aircraft?
What were the cost and price figures for this division?
clarifying_info.a: 10 years ago: fixed costs $450M/year, variable costs $1.8M/plane, selling price $2M/plane. Assume all figures are 10% higher today.

framework: Industry overview: current market size, growth trends, competitive landscape (Cessna and a small number of other players)
Financial analysis: market sizing (bottom-up and top-down), breakeven calculation, profit potential
Re-entry feasibility: startup costs to reopen plant, condition of existing assets, time to first sale
Internal capabilities: synergies with airplane engines BU, available talent, technology currency of 9-year-old plant
Risks: technology obsolescence, regulatory/FAA approval, fuel prices, economy, opportunity cost of selling assets
Recommendation: enter vs. divest, conditioned on market share achievability and risk tolerance

questions.prompt: How would you estimate the size of the recreational aircraft market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose both top-down (sum competitor revenues: Cessna + a few others) and bottom-up (estimate pilots → plane owners → annual purchases) approaches. Interviewer wants to see the bottom-up method in particular.

math.setup: Bottom-up: US population × pilot rate × income filter → individual buyers + club buyers → total planes ÷ useful life = annual demand
math.answer: Approximately 10,000 recreational aircraft purchased per year in the US.

questions.prompt: How many planes would the client need to sell per year to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for price and cost data, apply the 10% inflation, compute contribution margin per plane, then divide fixed costs by that margin to get breakeven volume. A strong candidate will also spontaneously convert the breakeven volume to a required market share.

math.setup: Adjusted price = $2M × 1.1; adjusted variable cost = $1.8M × 1.1; adjusted fixed cost = $450M × 1.1. Breakeven units = Fixed cost ÷ (Price − Variable cost).
math.answer: The client must sell 2,500 planes per year, requiring ~25% market share to break even.

questions.prompt: Do you think the client can capture 25% market share?
questions.guidance: Any well-reasoned answer is acceptable. Candidate should weigh the client's prior presence in the market, brand recognition, and synergies with the airplane engines BU against the 9-year gap, technology changes, and entrenched competitors like Cessna.

questions.prompt: What are the key risks of reopening the plant?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover multiple dimensions: operational (technology obsolescence after 9 years, plant maintenance and retooling time, finding trained personnel), market (economic downturn, fuel price spikes affecting demand), regulatory (FAA safety approval and flight testing delays), strategic (diversion of management focus from other BUs), and financial (opportunity cost of selling the plant vs. investing in re-entry).

brainstorming.prompt: What issues should the client consider when deciding whether to re-enter the recreational aircraft market?

categories.name: Market opportunity
ideas: Current market size and growth trajectory
Competitive landscape: Cessna and other incumbents
Demand drivers: pilot population trends, income levels, flying club growth

categories.name: Financial feasibility
ideas: Startup and retooling costs to reopen the plant
Profit potential at various volume levels
Opportunity cost: proceeds from selling assets

categories.name: Internal capabilities
ideas: Synergies with the airplane engines business unit
Availability of trained engineers and production staff
Currency of existing plant technology after 9 years idle
Speed to market from restart decision to first delivery

categories.name: Risks
ideas: Long lead time for maintenance, retooling, and hiring
FAA safety certification and flight testing delays
Diversion of management attention from core BUs

recommendation: Conduct a more detailed feasibility study before committing capital, focused on the actual cost to retool the plant and the realistic timeline to production
If retooling costs are manageable and the airplane engines BU can provide meaningful synergies, re-entry could be viable given a ~25% market share target
If the plant requires substantial capital investment or technology is too outdated, selling the assets and redeploying capital into higher-growth BUs is the better path
risks: Achieving 25% market share in a market dominated by established players like Cessna is aggressive
9 years of plant inactivity may require near-complete retooling, raising effective startup costs well above steady-state fixed costs
FAA re-certification could delay revenue generation by several years
A prolonged economic downturn (the case is set in 2009) could suppress recreational aircraft demand further
next_steps: Assess actual condition and retooling cost of the idle plant
Benchmark competitor market shares and identify likely response to new entrant
Model cash flows under optimistic, base, and downside volume scenarios
Evaluate asset sale value as the financial floor for the decision
